text: For the choirmaster; with stringed instruments, on the sheminith.\u1d43 A psalm of David.\n\nᵃ sheminith: a musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps an eight-stringed instrument or a lower octave.

versions.text: For the choirmaster; with stringed instruments, on the sheminith. A psalm of David.
versions.explanation: The transliterated term 'sheminith' will be opaque to hearers; a short footnote explaining that it is an uncertain musical term adds clarity without altering the text.

text: LORD, do not rebuke me in your anger, do not discipline me in your wrath.
Have mercy on me, LORD, for I am weak; heal me, LORD, for my bones are shaking.
My soul is shaken to the core. And you, LORD—how long?
Turn back, LORD, and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of your steadfast love.
For in death no one remembers you; who gives you thanks from Sheol?

versions.text: For in death no one remembers you; who praises you from the grave?
versions.explanation: The verb יוֹדֶה is specifically 'give thanks,' distinct from 'praise' (הלל), and שְׁאוֹל is the realm of the dead rather than a single burial place. If 'Sheol' is retained, a brief footnote such as 'Sheol: the realm of the dead' would help hearers.

text: I am worn out with my groaning. All night long I flood my bed; with my tears I drench my couch.

versions.text: I am worn out with groaning. All night long I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew places 'with my tears' (בְּדִמְעָתִי) only in the second line; the first line simply says 'every night I make my bed swim.' Adding 'with weeping' to the first clause introduces wording not in the text and blurs the two parallel lines. The revised form preserves the balanced parallelism and reads well aloud.

versions.text: I am worn out with groaning. All night long I flood my bed; I drench my couch with my tears.
versions.explanation: Two small gains: אַנְחָתִי carries the first-person suffix ('my groaning'), which the current rendering drops; and the Hebrew fronts בְּדִמְעָתִי ('with my tears') in the final line, so placing the phrase first mirrors the source and gives the closing line a stronger cadence for reading aloud.

text: My eyes are wasted with grief; they have grown weak because of all my foes.
Away from me, all you who do evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.
The LORD has heard my plea for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer.
All my enemies will be put to shame and utterly dismayed; they will turn back, shamed in an instant.
